To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-1 transducing activity can be induced by DNA damage-inducing agents.
DSBs are required for efficient HIV transduction in both dividing and nondividing cells.
HIV-1 transducing activity is increased in nondividing host cells by the introduction of double-strand DNA breaks in the host cell genome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how HIV-1 is transduced into nondividing cells and the role of DNA repair proteins in HIV-1 transductions.
the development of new and more efficient gene delivery methods.
the identification of novel cellular co-factors that are required for HIV-1 transfection and integration into the host cell chromosome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DSB-inducing drugs up-regulate HIV-1 transfection in non-dividing cells by inducing the expression and/or the activation of cellular DSB repair proteins.
DSB-inducing treatment of nondividing cells up-regulates HIV-1 transfection efficiency.
DNA repair proteins are required for efficient HIV infection and that these proteins are induced by DSBs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-1 transductions can be enhanced by the introduction of DNA damage into the host cell, but that this enhancement is not a result of a general enhancement of DNA repair.
HIV-1 transductions in nondividing or differentiated cells can be enhanced by inducing the expression of cellular DNA repair proteins.
HIV-1 transduces cells more efficiently when DSB repair proteins, such as DNA-PK, are up-regulated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DSB-inducing drugs are useful tools to enhance HIV-1 transductions in nondividing and differentiated cells.
DNA damage repair proteins play a key role in the early steps in the retroviral lifecycle.
DSB-inducing treatments are effective in increasing HIV-1 transgene expression in nondividing cell populations.
